name: Ukraine
governanceModel: Bottom-up, innovation-first — voluntary self-regulation bridging toward an EU AI Act-aligned law, alongside a fast-moving wartime defence-AI sector
debateTopics: Wartime defence AI and autonomous weapons
Bottom-up self-regulation before an EU-aligned law
Balancing EU AI Act alignment with an innovation-first economy
overview:
Ukraine occupies an unusual position in AI governance: a candidate for EU membership committed in principle to aligning with the EU AI Act, yet pursuing a deliberately 'bottom-up', innovation-first path to regulation while simultaneously running one of the world's most intensive real-world laboratories for defence AI. Its domestic-policy approach, set out in an AI Regulation Roadmap published in October 2023 by Vice Prime Minister and Minister for Digital Transformation Mykhailo Fedorov, sequences voluntary measures — a White Paper and a voluntary code of conduct (endorsed December 2024) — ahead of a binding, EU-harmonised law, giving businesses time to prepare.

The war with Russia has made Ukraine a global focal point for applied and defence AI. The government-backed Brave1 cluster coordinates hundreds of companies building AI-enabled drones, computer-vision targeting, electronic-warfare countermeasures and battlefield-data systems, and the state has pushed AI into public services through Diia.AI, described as the first national-government AI agent for citizen services. Ukraine's civilian tech sector — home to companies such as Grammarly, GitLab, MacPaw, Preply and voice-AI firm Respeecher — remains internationally significant despite the war. The governance challenge is to reconcile a light-touch, growth-oriented domestic stance with the obligations of EU accession and the hard ethical questions raised by increasingly autonomous weapons.

currentDirection.summary: Ukraine's civilian AI-governance stance remains deliberately light and innovation-first — voluntary self-regulation as a bridge to an EU-aligned law rather than early binding rules — a posture largely unchanged through 2026. The most dynamic movement is in defence AI, where institutions such as Brave1 and its Dataroom are scaling fast; the medium-term tightening will come from EU accession, which will eventually require transposition of the EU AI Act.

recentDevelopments.text: The Ministry of Economy, Environment and Agriculture agreed with Kyivstar and VEON (30 June 2026) to pursue a sovereign AI data centre in Ukraine, so that data for AI solutions is processed and stored domestically rather than on foreign servers. The government framed the project as a step toward technological sovereignty under the national AI strategy's goal of placing Ukraine among the world's top three countries for public-sector AI by 2030.

The Ministry of Defence launched the Defense AI Center A1 (17 March 2026), its first centre of excellence dedicated to integrating artificial intelligence across the Defence Forces, established with UK government backing. Led by CEO Danylo Tsvok, the centre is tasked with analyzing combat data, forecasting Russian actions, developing autonomous systems, and building AI-enabled command-and-control tools -- the first in a planned network of military-technology centres of excellence.

Ukraine opened the Brave1 Dataroom (January 2026), a shared platform — built with the Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Digital Transformation, the Armed Forces and US firm Palantir — to let defence companies train AI models on battlefield data; reporting indicates 100+ companies were using it within months.
The EU and Ukraine launched a new €3.3m BRAVE1 grant programme under the EU4UA Defence Tech initiative, with an early round focused on high-speed drone interceptors and radar systems.

Reporting indicates Ukraine's defence-AI ecosystem now spans 200+ companies developing drone and autonomy technologies, with dozens of AI and computer-vision systems in frontline use (autonomous targeting, detection of camouflaged equipment, battlefield-data analysis via systems such as Delta), coordinated through the Brave1 cluster.

MacPaw and voice-AI firm Respeecher announced (at CES 2026) a partnership to give MacPaw's new 'Eney' AI assistant a synthesised voice — one of several signs that Ukraine's civilian product-IT sector is reorienting around AI despite the war.

The government expanded Diia.AI, launched in autumn 2025 and described as the first national-government AI agent for citizen services; built by Ukrainian firm Kitsoft on Google's Gemini model, it delivers routine bureaucratic services through the Diia app.

Ukraine's Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Ethical and Responsible Use of AI — the first stage of the 2023 AI Regulation Roadmap — was endorsed in December 2024, with leading domestic technology companies committing to transparency, fairness, safety and data-protection principles ahead of any binding, EU-aligned law.

policyAndRegulation.title: AI Regulation Roadmap
policyAndRegulation.summary: Published in October 2023 by the Ministry of Digital Transformation, the roadmap sets a bottom-up, phased path to AI regulation: first non-binding tools (a White Paper and a voluntary code of conduct) plus capacity-building, then a comprehensive law harmonised with the EU AI Act. The sequencing is designed to let Ukrainian businesses adapt before binding obligations arrive.

policyAndRegulation.title: Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Ethical and Responsible Use of AI
policyAndRegulation.summary: Endorsed December 2024 as the first substantive deliverable of the roadmap. Signatory technology companies voluntarily commit to unified ethical principles — transparency, fairness, safety and data protection — pending a future binding framework aligned with the EU AI Act.

policyAndRegulation.title: EU AI Act-aligned law (planned)
policyAndRegulation.summary: The roadmap's second phase envisages a comprehensive AI law modelled on the EU AI Act, to bring Ukraine into line with EU legal regimes as part of its accession process. As of mid-2026 this remains a planned, not-yet-adopted framework; the White Paper and voluntary code are intended as the bridge to it.

researchEcosystem.summary: Ukraine's AI strength is heavily applied rather than frontier: a large civilian product-IT sector (Grammarly, GitLab, MacPaw, Preply, Respeecher and others) plus a fast-scaling defence-AI ecosystem coordinated through Brave1 and Diia.City incentives. Universities such as the Kyiv-based technical schools supply talent, but war-driven disruption, mobilisation and emigration weigh on the academic research base; much cutting-edge work happens inside companies and defence-tech units rather than laboratories.

notableGaps.note: As of mid-2026 Ukraine has no binding, comprehensive AI law — only a voluntary code and White Paper. A binding, EU AI Act-aligned framework is planned as part of accession but not yet adopted, leaving civilian AI governance largely self-regulatory for now.

Ukraine has no domestic frontier or near-frontier model developer; flagship civilian AI products and the Diia.AI agent build on foreign foundation models (e.g. Google's Gemini). Its distinctive strength is applied and defence AI, not model training at scale.

The rapid battlefield deployment of increasingly autonomous drones and targeting systems has outpaced any settled domestic or international governance framework for lethal autonomy — a genuine and openly acknowledged gap rather than a policy choice.

debates.topic: Wartime defence AI and autonomous weapons
debates.summary: Ukraine has become a live test bed for AI-enabled autonomous weapons, raising acute questions — for Ukraine and the wider world — about human control, accountability and the pace at which lethal autonomy is being fielded.
debates.expanded: Coordinated through Brave1 and its Dataroom, hundreds of companies are building AI-driven drone targeting, computer-vision detection and swarm-coordination systems, some reportedly automating large parts of the interception or strike chain. Supporters argue these tools are essential to Ukraine's defence and are being developed responsibly under intense operational pressure; critics and arms-control analysts warn that battlefield deployment is outrunning any agreed framework for meaningful human control over lethal autonomous systems. The debate has global stakes, as Ukraine's experience shapes Western military-AI doctrine.

debates.topic: Bottom-up self-regulation before an EU-aligned law
debates.summary: Ukraine has deliberately chosen voluntary self-regulation — a White Paper and code of conduct — as a bridge to a binding, EU AI Act-aligned law, betting that light early rules protect innovation without abandoning EU alignment.
debates.expanded: The 2023 AI Regulation Roadmap sequences non-binding tools and capacity-building ahead of legislation, explicitly to give a war-strained economy and a fast-moving tech sector time to adapt. Proponents see this as pragmatic and innovation-friendly; sceptics ask whether voluntary commitments are enough in the interim, and whether accession pressures will force a faster, more prescriptive transposition of the EU AI Act than the gradualist roadmap envisages.

debates.topic: Balancing EU AI Act alignment with an innovation-first economy
debates.summary: As an EU accession candidate, Ukraine must eventually adopt EU AI Act obligations, testing whether harmonisation can be reconciled with the light-touch, growth-oriented approach that suits its wartime tech and defence sectors.
debates.expanded: EU membership will require Ukraine to transpose the AI Act, including risk-tiered obligations and (for general-purpose AI) transparency duties. Ukrainian policymakers have signalled they want to preserve an innovation-first environment — especially for defence tech, much of which sits outside or at the edge of civilian AI rules. The open question is how much friction arises between EU harmonisation and a domestic ecosystem optimised for speed, and whether Ukraine can shape EU rules to accommodate its distinctive defence-AI experience.
